summary:
Lima stands under the national framework of Peru: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. A trans visitor to the capital faces rules set in Lima rather than in the Metropolitan Municipality of Lima itself.

In February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia; the fused text was approved in plenary on 2 April 2025 with custody, medical, caregiving and disability exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by "biological sex", barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity", and the text obliges removal of "ambiguous" signage of the kind Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport had placed, reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity".

Enforcement was anticipated at the door. Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, warned that security staff will judge who may enter a bathroom on the basis of identity documents (DNI), an approach she calls discriminatory and founded on prejudice. The restriction also reaches private premises: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Violence in the capital follows the recorded national pattern. The observatory counted 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 reported rights violations across Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women most affected and 30 of the 54 dead. Nineteen homicides were recorded in 2023 alone, and no suspects have been identified in 26 of the killings. On 12 February 2023 the "Los Gallegos" gang abducted the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, from jirón Chancay in central Lima and shot her dead with roughly 30 rounds, an example of the pattern recorded in the capital.

The state keeps no system recording the sexual orientation or gender identity of people killed, and co-author Gianna Camacho of the 2024 report on rising hate crimes stressed that published figures are only a sub-registry.

Hate-crime law offers no cover. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is left one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two findings by the Inter-American system constrain the regime. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation: Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found that the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks.
